metadata.file_name: 72. Teig. (2024). Uncovering Student Strategies for Solving Scientific Inquiry Tasks: Insights from Student Process Data in PISA.pdf
metadata.title: Uncovering Student Strategies for Solving Scientific Inquiry Tasks: Insights from Student Process Data in PISA

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses publicly available PISA 2015 process-log data and a small PISA 2015 field-trial subset (Task 1 in Norway; Example 2 in Norway). The manuscript does not report applying PISA complex survey weights (e.g., student/sampling weights) or replicate-weight procedures, and it does not name any weight variables. Because the analyses are person-centered (latent profile analysis) and process-mining visualization on log-derived indicators rather than PV-based achievement modeling, the paper provides no explicit guidance on weight use for inference. For replication with full PISA microdata, analysts should consult the OECD PISA technical documentation for appropriate student weights and replicate weights, and then decide whether to incorporate them into profile estimation and group comparisons.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables in this paper are derived from process-log indicators (e.g., number of actions/trials, time-on-task, time before first action) and from task response components used to define accuracy categories/profiles, rather than PV-based cognitive achievement scores. As a result, PISA plausible values are not the target of the modeling, so PV handling is not applicable. The manuscript mentions preprocessing steps including handling missing data, but it does not specify the missing-data rule (e.g., listwise deletion, imputation) used for the analytic datasets, which is a reporting gap for reproducibility.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Example 1 uses the PISA 2015 field trial in Norway and restricts to 10th-grade students assigned to the assessment unit Running in Hot Weather; within that unit it analyzes Task 1 (second question) and further restricts to students with log data for the task (N=81). Example 2 uses PISA 2015 data from Norway and analyzes Grade 9 and Grade 10 students (0.8% Grade 9; 99.2% Grade 10) from 221 schools, using a modified released field-trial item (Task 2) and nine student-questionnaire items capturing inquiry-based teaching and learning practices; the analytic sample for Task 2 is N=1222.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 Field Trial (Norway) Grade 10 Science — Task 1 (Running in Hot Weather)
main_findings.target_variable: Inquiry task performance profile indicators (correct/partial/incorrect) via process-mining sequences
main_findings.performance_metrics: Not reported (process-mining visualization; descriptive means and proportions). Key proportions: 63.7% used VOTAT; only 40.7% of VOTAT users solved correctly. Group sizes: correct N=33, partially correct N=30, incorrect N=17.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 Field Trial (Norway) Grade 10 Science data for Task 1, the study leveraged VOTAT navigation behavior, number of actions/trials, and response-time indicators to characterize how students’ log-derived sequences relate to correct, partially correct, and incorrect inquiry performance, finding that many students used VOTAT but only 40.7% of those achieved full correctness. This indicates that instruction should not only encourage VOTAT use but also support students in planning and executing the univariable-to-evidence coordination needed to complete the task successfully, while recognizing that process patterns alone do not guarantee correct scientific reasoning.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 (Norway) Grade 9/10 Science — Task 2 (modified Running in Hot Weather field-trial item)
main_findings.target_variable: Inquiry performance latent profiles (strategic vs emergent vs disengaged) from process-log indicators
main_findings.performance_metrics: Latent profile analysis: three-profile solution with significant VLMR and LMR-LRT tests; high entropy and distinct class separation/homogeneity (exact values not reported). Descriptive profile means: Strategic Maction=14.99, Mtrial=4.58, Mtime-before-first-action=31.69s, Mtime-on-task=186.58s; Emergent Mtime-on-task=102.59s; Disengaged Mtime-on-task=43.97s. Transfer to multivariable VOTAT: 38.7% showed high probability of adapting VOTAT into multivariable context. Additional analysis (Association between inquiry-teaching practices and inquiry performance profiles (MANOVA profile mean differences)): MANOVA with Bonferroni post hoc comparisons (Table 3): Debate differentiated all three profiles (F=17.53, p<.01; pairwise: 1>3, 1>2, 2>3). Several items showed strategic>disengaged and/or emergent>disengaged differences: Lab (F=5.18, p<.01; 1>3), Draw (F=9.42, p<.01; 1>3, 2>3), Idea (F=5.56, p<.01; 1>3), Design (F=4.72, p<.01; 1>3), Test (F=3.17, p<.01; 1>3). No significant differences for Explain, Argue, and Concept across profiles (per text).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 (Norway) Grade 9/10 Science data for Task 2, the study leveraged interactive strategy use and log-derived exploration and timing indicators to identify three latent inquiry-performance profiles, finding that the strategic profile showed the highest likelihood of using the interactive strategy and the highest time-on-task and exploration, while emergent students took longer but still had low probabilities of explaining claim–evidence relationships. This indicates that classroom support should target both multivariable coordination and the explicit claim–evidence linking process, not merely increasing exploration time or strategy attempts.

data.outcome_summary: This paper demonstrates how PISA process-log data can be used to study scientific inquiry strategies beyond product correctness. In Example 1, process mining (Disco with the fuzzy miner algorithm) was applied to PISA 2015 field-trial Task 1 in Norway (N=81) to visualize students’ simulation interaction sequences; 63.7% used the VOTAT strategy, yet only 40.7% of those achieved full correctness, highlighting difficulties in coordinating evidence with claims. In Example 2, latent profile analysis on log-derived indicators for Task 2 in PISA 2015 Norway (N=1222) identified three profiles (strategic, emergent, disengaged), with strategic students showing the highest exploration and time-on-task and the highest likelihood of successful inquiry. MANOVA results linked inquiry-based teaching practices to profile membership, with class debate about investigations differentiating all three profiles. Limitations include the absence of reported PV handling, missing-data rules, and survey-weight application details, and the fact that the methods are profiling/visualization rather than predictive ML.
